summary: Defines an RTCP packet type and an RTCP XR block type for Inter-Destination Media Synchronization, which keeps playout in step across several receivers. Participants report playout information, and a settings packet distributes a common target playout point. Use cases include social TV and networked loudspeakers.

eli5.summary: Friends in different homes watch the same show and want to see each moment at the same time. This lets their players compare notes and line up.

questions: how to sync playback across devices rtp
how to synchronize playout across devices with rtcp
subtitle: How receivers in different places use RTCP to play the same stream at the same moment.

tldr.problem: When people in different places watch or hear the same live stream, their playout drifts apart because each path and device adds a different delay. One friend sees the goal well before the other.
tldr.mechanism: Receivers send an RTCP XR IDMS Report Block saying when they got and optionally played a given RTP packet. A server summarizes these reports and sends back an RTCP IDMS Settings Packet (packet type 211) with a common target playout point.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can adjust their playout buffers to meet that shared point. The RFC leaves the actual synchronization algorithm out of scope and requires receivers to have synchronized wallclocks.

today: RFC 7272 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the RTCP packet type and XR block for IDMS, and relies on RFC 7273 for signaling clock sources.

sections.title: What IDMS Is and Why It Is Needed
sections.content:
Inter-Destination Media Synchronization (IDMS) means playing media streams at two or more geographically distributed places in a time-synchronized way. It works for unicast and multicast streams and for audio, video and text such as subtitles.

The RFC lists several use cases. In social TV, people at different locations watch the same broadcast while talking to each other, and a skew in playout spoils the experience (the example is one friend seeing a football goal well before another). A networked video wall tiles several screens into one picture, and unsynchronized refresh breaks the illusion of a single image. Networked loudspeakers need even more accuracy because people are more sensitive to audio delay than to video delay, possibly in the range of microseconds.

RTCP is a good carrier because arrival and presentation times of RTP packets can be seen as reception quality feedback, which RTCP already carries. The specification is independent of the synchronization algorithm, which is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If friends watch the same match in different homes, one may shout 'goal!' while the other has not seen it yet. IDMS is a way to make everyone see things together.

sections.title: A Typical IDMS Session
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an example. Alice invites Bob to watch a football game together, and the invitation carries a link to the media server and a unique sync-group identifier. Both clients receive RTP packets from the media server and send periodic RTCP receiver reports.

In addition, each client periodically sends an RTCP XR IDMS Report Block to the Sync Server function of the media server, with timestamps for when it received, and optionally played out, a particular RTP packet. The server works out a reference client, for example the most lagged one, and sends an RTCP IDMS Settings Packet with that client's playout information to both.

In the example Bob has the longest delay, so Bob's client does nothing. Alice's client may temporarily decrease its playout rate until it matches, or simply pause until it catches up. The exact algorithm is up to the client, and other algorithms may add even more delay than the most delayed client has, for example to absorb delay variation or new clients joining.
sections.eli5: Both friends tell the helper when they saw a moment. The helper finds who is behind. The friend who is ahead slows down a bit until both match.

sections.title: The Two Roles: MSAS and SC
sections.content:
The design is based on a sync-maestro architecture with two roles. The Synchronization Client (SC) reports RTP packet arrival and presentation times, can receive IDMS Settings Packets and uses them to adjust its playout buffer. The Media Synchronization Application Server (MSAS) collects the reports from the SCs in a synchronization group and distributes a summary as settings, for example using the most lagged SC's times.

The diagram shows the MSAS as part of the RTP sender, but that is not required. It might be an independent function in the network, or one of the SC devices might also act as the MSAS in a master/slave arrangement. Wherever it sits, the MSAS must have access to the RTP stream the reports apply to, so it can correlate reports from different SCs.

Two message types connect them: the RTCP XR IDMS Report Block goes from SC to MSAS, and the new RTCP IDMS Settings Packet goes from MSAS to SC.
sections.eli5: The clients are the friends watching. The MSAS is the helper who collects everyone's notes and tells them how to line up.

sections.title: The RTCP XR IDMS Report Block
sections.content:
The report block is a new RTCP XR block type with BT=12. It has a fixed length: 8 32-bit words, with the block length field set to 7. Its fields are:

  • SPST (4 bits): the role of the sender. Value 1 means the sender is an SC; 2 to 4 are defined by ETSI TISPAN; 5 to 15 are unassigned.
  • P flag (1 bit): set to 1 if the Packet Presented NTP timestamp holds a value. If 0, receivers SHALL ignore that field.
  • PT (7 bits): the payload type of the reported RTP packet, needed when the MSAS is a third party so it can relate timestamps from different SCs.
  • Media Stream Correlation Identifier (32 bits): for an SC this carries the Synchronization Group Identifier (SyncGroupId). The value 0 means empty and all ones is reserved.
  • SSRC of media source (32 bits), Packet Received NTP timestamp (64 bits, wallclock arrival of the first octet), Packet Received RTP timestamp (32 bits) and Packet Presented NTP timestamp (32 bits).

The presented timestamp is the time the rendered media unit reached the user, and consists of the least significant 16 bits of the NTP seconds and the most significant 16 bits of the fraction. If none is available, it is set to 0 along with the P flag. Reserved bits MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

When several consecutive RTP packets share a timestamp, an SC SHOULD report on the one it received with the lowest sequence number, so two receivers do not accidentally report on different packets of the same frame. The RFC adds no new rules for when to send reports; the existing RFC 3550 timing rules apply, and an SC SHOULD report on a packet received since the last report.
sections.eli5: The report is a short form: which packet I am talking about, what time it arrived, and, if I know it, what time it actually showed on my screen.

sections.title: The IDMS Settings Packet
sections.content:
The MSAS answers with a new RTCP packet type, PT=211, registered with IANA. The first 64 bits are the standard RTCP header, including the SSRC of the packet sender. The rest of the packet carries the SSRC of the media source, the Media Stream Correlation Identifier (the SyncGroupId the packet is sent to), the Packet Received NTP timestamp (64 bits), the Packet Received RTP timestamp (32 bits) and the Packet Presented NTP timestamp (64 bits).

These values describe the reference client: when it received, and optionally presented, a real or hypothetical RTP packet chosen by the MSAS. Receivers use them to set their playout delay. Because RTP timestamps wrap around, the sender MUST use recent NTP values that are not so far in the past or future as to be ambiguous. The Presented field is set to 0 when empty and MAY be left empty if none or only one receiver reported presentation times.

The settings packet has a 64-bit presented timestamp while the report block has only 32 bits. The RFC explains that some uses, such as phased array transducers, need very precise control, while an MSAS will in practice add extra delay for jitter on top of the most lagged receiver, so 32 bits suffice for reports.
sections.eli5: The helper's reply says 'here is the moment to match: this packet, seen at this time, shown at this time'. Each friend then adjusts to it.

sections.title: Clocks and Presentation Timestamps
sections.content:
Everything depends on receivers having synchronized wallclocks, since reports from different receivers are only comparable on a common timeline. For social TV, accuracy on the order of hundreds of milliseconds is enough, and correct use of NTP on receivers will in most situations achieve it. Receivers should synchronize at the start of a session and, for high accuracy, repeatedly during it.

For stricter needs such as audio, the global NTP system may not be sufficient. The RFC suggests a local NTP server, GPS time or the Precision Time Protocol (IEEE 1588-2008). SCs MAY use RFC 7273 to signal which clock sources they use or have available. IDMS is sensitive to leap-second discrepancies when relying on NTP, so following the guidelines in RFC 7164 is RECOMMENDED.

A receiver SHALL report arrival times and MAY report playout times. Synchronizing on arrival times can lose some accuracy but is adequate for many applications such as social TV; if receivers are controlled with the same buffer settings and decoding and rendering times, high accuracy can be achieved. Reporting presentation times is more accurate, and whether to implement it is up to the application.
sections.eli5: For this to work, everybody's watch must show the same time. Otherwise 'I saw it at 7:00' means different things to different people.

sections.title: Signaling with SDP
sections.content:
Use of IDMS is signaled with a new media-level SDP attribute, rtcp-idms, which also carries the sync-group identifier. The ABNF is rtcp-idms = "a=" "rtcp-idms" ":" sync-grp CRLF, with sync-grp = "sync-group=" SyncGroupId. The example is a=rtcp-idms:sync-group=42. The SyncGroupId is a 32-bit unsigned decimal; 0 means empty and 4294967295 is reserved. When several related streams exist, IDMS is done on one of them, preferably audio over video, and the rest follow with existing inter-stream synchronization.

In an offer/answer exchange, the receiver (the SC) inserts the attribute in its offer, using a predetermined SyncGroupId if it has one, or 0 if it does not know. The sender SHALL include the attribute in its answer. If the offer had a non-empty ID the sender SHOULD NOT change it; if it was empty the sender SHALL fill in the proper one, or remove the attribute if it cannot. A sender may also add the attribute on its own to an offer that lacked it. A receiver that sees the attribute in an answer SHALL start sending XR IDMS reports and be ready to receive settings. A later update that omits the attribute ends participation, and one with a different SyncGroupId switches groups.

In declarative cases with no offer/answer, the MSAS just inserts the attribute and a valid SyncGroupId, and receivers SHALL start reporting.
sections.eli5: Before the show starts, each player says 'I want to join group 42'. Once the server agrees, they begin sending notes and listening for the helper's instructions.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3611 apply. The main concern is bad data, accidental or malicious: if one device reports a two-hour delayed playout, others in the group could decide to delay by two hours too. The RFC says SCs and MSASs should check for out-of-bound information, for example differences in playout time exceeding configured limits such as more than ten seconds.

Implementations can also add source authentication and message integrity, and RFC 7201 gives an overview of the options in RTP environments. Message confidentiality additionally prevents third parties from learning, via the Media Stream Correlation Identifier, that hosts are receiving the same stream.

Another weak point is the clock synchronization method. If an attacker adjusts an SC's wallclock, that SC reports wrong values, so the RFC recommends a secure time synchronization service.
sections.eli5: If one friend lies and says 'my show is two hours behind', everyone might wait for them. So players should ignore reports that look crazy.

fields.name: SPST
fields.desc: Role of the packet sender; 1 means an SC.

fields.name: P
fields.desc: 1 if the Packet Presented NTP timestamp holds a value.

fields.name: PT
fields.desc: Payload type of the reported RTP packet.

fields.name: Media Stream Correlation Identifier
fields.desc: Carries the SyncGroupId when the sender is an SC.

fields.name: SSRC of media source
fields.desc: SSRC from the RTP header of the reported packet.

fields.name: Packet Received NTP timestamp
fields.desc: Wallclock arrival time of the packet's first octet.

fields.name: Packet Received RTP timestamp
fields.desc: RTP timestamp of the reported packet.

fields.name: Packet Presented NTP timestamp
fields.desc: Time the media unit was presented to the user; 0 if unavailable.
